question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

France is a largest country.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. large.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence contains the indefinite article "a". An indefinite article can never be used with a superlative degree, because a superlative singles out one particular thing and therefore demands the definite article "the" (the largest, the smallest, the best).

◦ Incorrect: France is a largest country.

◦ Correct: France is a large country.

• Here there is no comparison at all in the sentence — no "than" and no group is mentioned. So the positive degree "large" is the only grammatically fit option.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "smaller" and Option 2 "larger" are comparative forms; a comparative needs "than" (France is larger than Nepal), which is absent here.

• Option 3 "smallest" is a superlative and repeats the very error of the original sentence — it would still need "the", and it also reverses the sense.

NOTE

• Degrees of comparison: large – larger – largest.

◦ Positive: used when no comparison is made — "France is a large country."

◦ Comparative: used to compare two things, always with "than" — "France is larger than Italy."

◦ Superlative: used to compare more than two, always with "the" — "Russia is the largest country in the world."

• Rule to remember: a/an + superlative = wrong; the + superlative = right.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.

Mr Sharma would have left / the station / by this time / tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Mr Sharma would have left.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The time marker "by this time tomorrow" points to a moment in the future. An action that will be completed before a given future time must be expressed in the future perfect tense — "will have + V3".

◦ Incorrect: Mr Sharma would have left the station by this time tomorrow.

◦ Correct: Mr Sharma will have left the station by this time tomorrow.

• "Would have + V3" is a past unreal/conditional form (used for something that did not actually happen — "He would have left if he had got a ticket"). It clashes with the future adverbial "tomorrow".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "the station" is a correct noun phrase with the definite article.

• "by this time" is the correct prepositional phrase for a deadline ("by" = not later than).

• "tomorrow" is the correct future adverb of time and needs no preposition.

NOTE

• Future perfect = will/shall have + past participle. Signal words: by tomorrow, by next month, by 2030, by the time, by then.

◦ By next June, she will have completed her degree.

• Do not confuse: will have + V3 (future perfect) vs would have + V3 (unfulfilled past condition, third conditional).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.

“Do not turn a blind eye to all the mischief your child is up to”, the teacher told the young parent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Pretend not to notice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to turn a blind eye (to something)" means to deliberately ignore something wrong; to pretend not to see or notice it. (जानबूझकर अनदेखा करना)

◦ In the sentence the teacher warns the parent not to ignore the child's mischief — i.e., not to pretend not to notice it.

◦ Example: The guard turned a blind eye to the students sneaking out.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Close the door" is a literal action and has nothing to do with ignoring wrongdoing.

• Option 2 "Take pride in" means to feel satisfaction about something — the opposite of ignoring.

• Option 3 "Give rewards" means to reward, which does not match "Do not ..." in a warning about mischief.

NOTE

• Origin: the phrase is popularly traced to Admiral Horatio Nelson, who is said to have put his telescope to his blind eye at the Battle of Copenhagen (1801) so that he could claim not to have seen the signal to retreat.

• Related idioms of ignoring: "look the other way", "turn a deaf ear" (refuse to listen), "sweep under the carpet" (hide a problem), "give the cold shoulder" (ignore a person deliberately).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The mother ________ the chips because they were soggy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. discarded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Discard" means to throw away / get rid of something that is no longer wanted or is unfit for use. (फेंक देना)

• The reason clause "because they were soggy" (limp, damp and unappetising) explains why the chips had to be thrown away.

◦ Correct: The mother discarded the chips because they were soggy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "saved" (kept for later) contradicts the reason given — nobody keeps soggy chips.

• Option 2 "wasted" means to use carelessly/squander; it usually needs an object like money, time or an opportunity, and it blames the mother rather than describing disposal. It does not fit the logic of "because they were soggy".

• Option 4 "recovered" (got back something lost) is illogical here.

NOTE

• Synonyms of discard: throw away, dispose of, jettison, dump, scrap, cast off. Antonyms: keep, retain, preserve, save.

• Word usage: "soggy" = unpleasantly wet and soft (सीला हुआ); its opposite for snacks is "crisp/crunchy".

question:
Identify the most appropriate meaning of the given word.

Hope
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Wish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hope" means a feeling of expectation and desire for a particular thing to happen; to want something to be true. Its closest meaning among the options is "wish" — a desire for something. (आशा / इच्छा)

◦ Example: I hope/wish to see you soon.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Caution" means care taken to avoid danger (सावधानी) — unrelated.

• Option 2 "Realism" means seeing and accepting things as they really are (यथार्थवाद) — it is about facts, not desire.

• Option 3 "Cynicism" means a distrustful, negative attitude that believes people act only from selfish motives (निंदावाद) — it is the opposite in spirit to hope.

NOTE

• Synonyms of hope: wish, desire, aspiration, expectation, optimism, longing, anticipation.

• Antonyms of hope: despair, hopelessness, pessimism, cynicism, dejection.

• Grammar note: "hope" is followed by a that-clause or a to-infinitive ("I hope that he wins", "I hope to win"), whereas "wish" for an unreal situation takes the past subjunctive ("I wish I were rich").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Have egg on your face
option_2: To be made to look foolish or embarrassed
option_3: Making a choice between two unpleasant choices
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To be made to look foolish or embarrassed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to have egg on one's face" means to be made to look foolish, embarrassed or humiliated, usually because of something one said or did that went wrong. (शर्मिंदा होना / मूर्ख दिखना)

◦ Example: The minister had egg on his face when his own figures were proved wrong in Parliament.

• The image behind it is of a person who has literally been hit with an egg — publicly ridiculed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Defeat someone thoroughly" is the meaning of idioms like "beat hollow" / "wipe the floor with someone".

• Option 3 "Making a choice between two unpleasant choices" is the meaning of "between the devil and the deep blue sea" or "Hobson's choice / a catch-22".

• Option 4 "Reveal a secret" is the meaning of "let the cat out of the bag" or "spill the beans".

NOTE

• Related idioms of embarrassment: "red-faced", "eat humble pie" (to admit one was wrong and apologise), "eat one's words", "lose face" (to lose respect).

question:
The following sentence contains some errors. Select the option that correctly rectifies the error.

The tiger was tranquiliized in the morning and keept in a cage to avoid disturbannces by human beings.
option_1: The tiger was tranquilized in the morning and kept in a cage to avoiid disturbaences by human beings.
option_2: The tiger was tranquilized in the morning and kept in a cage to avoid disturbances by human beings.
option_3: The tiger was traanquilized in the morning and kept in a cage to avoid dissturbances by human beings.
option_4: The tiger was tranquiliized in the morning and keept in a cage to avoid disturbances by human beings.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The tiger was tranquilized in the morning and kept in a cage to avoid disturbances by human beings.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence contains three spelling errors: "tranquiliized", "keept" and "disturbannces". The option that corrects all three at once, without introducing any new mistake, is the right answer.

◦ "tranquiliized" → "tranquilized" (made calm/sedated with a drug)

◦ "keept" → "kept" (past tense of "keep": keep – kept – kept)

◦ "disturbannces" → "disturbances" (interruptions/disorder)

• Only Option 2 is completely error-free: "The tiger was tranquilized in the morning and kept in a cage to avoid disturbances by human beings."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 corrects "tranquilized" and "kept" but adds two new errors — "avoiid" and "disturbaences".

• Option 3 wrongly spells "traanquilized" and "dissturbances".

• Option 4 leaves the original errors "tranquiliized" and "keept" untouched.

NOTE

• Strategy for such questions: mark each misspelt word in the question sentence, then reject every option that still carries an error or that adds a fresh one; exactly one option will be clean.

• Spelling note: "tranquilize/tranquilise" (American "tranquilizer", British "tranquilliser") comes from "tranquil" = calm and peaceful.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.

She’s reading a ________(secrecy) novel and can’t wait to find out who the killer is.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. mystery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed clue word is "secrecy" — the state of keeping something hidden or unknown. The word that carries this sense and also names a type of novel is "mystery". (रहस्य)

• The second half of the sentence, "can't wait to find out who the killer is", is the classic description of a mystery novel (a whodunit).

◦ Correct: She's reading a mystery novel and can't wait to find out who the killer is.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "crisis" means a time of intense difficulty or danger (संकट) — there is no such collocation as a "crisis novel".

• Option 2 "complication" means something that makes a situation more difficult (जटिलता) — it does not mean secrecy.

• Option 3 "difficulty" means hardship or trouble (कठिनाई) — again unrelated to something hidden.

NOTE

• Synonyms of mystery: enigma, riddle, puzzle, secret, conundrum.

• Genres of fiction often asked in SSC exams: mystery/thriller (suspense, crime), fiction, non-fiction, science fiction, fantasy, biography/autobiography, satire.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.

The viable of life / depends on a pair / of conflicting realities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The viable of life.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Viable" is an adjective (meaning capable of working successfully / able to survive). After the definite article "The" and before "of life", the sentence needs a noun, not an adjective.

• The correct noun form is "viability" (the ability to survive or succeed).

◦ Incorrect: The viable of life depends on a pair of conflicting realities.

◦ Correct: The viability of life depends on a pair of conflicting realities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "depends on a pair" is correct — the verb "depend" always takes the preposition "on/upon".

• "of conflicting realities" is a correct prepositional phrase ("conflicting" is a participial adjective before the plural noun "realities").

• Since a clear error exists, "No error" (Option 2) cannot be chosen.

NOTE

• Word-form family: viable (adjective) – viability (noun) – viably (adverb).

• Similar adjective → noun conversions often tested: able → ability, stable → stability, probable → probability, responsible → responsibility, flexible → flexibility.

• Rule: after "the ... of", a noun is required (the strength of, the beauty of, the viability of).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

I shall be playing for four hours.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. shall be playing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "for four hours" states the duration of an action. When a period of time introduced by "for" is mentioned, the continuous tense must be replaced by the perfect continuous tense.

• So the future continuous "shall be playing" must become the future perfect continuous "shall have been playing".

◦ Incorrect: I shall be playing for four hours.

◦ Correct: I shall have been playing for four hours.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "I" is the correct first-person subject pronoun and correctly takes "shall".

• "for" is the correct preposition before a period of time.

• "four hours" is a correct plural time expression.

NOTE

• Rule: since/for + time with a continuing action requires the perfect continuous tense.

◦ Present perfect continuous: He has been playing for four hours.

◦ Past perfect continuous: He had been playing for four hours.

◦ Future perfect continuous: He will/shall have been playing for four hours.

• "Since" is used with a point of time (since 5 o'clock, since Monday) and "for" with a period of time (for four hours, for two years).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Our team is all on the same page when it comes to our goals for the upcoming project.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Be in agreement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to be on the same page" means to be in agreement; to share the same understanding, opinion or plan about something. (एकमत होना)

◦ In the sentence, the whole team agrees about the goals of the coming project.

◦ Example: Before we start work, let us make sure everyone is on the same page.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Be confused" and Option 3 "Be unsure" describe a lack of clarity, not agreement.

• Option 4 "Be in conflict" is the opposite of the idiom's meaning.

NOTE

• The image behind the idiom is of several people reading from the very same page of a book, so they see exactly the same thing.

• Similar idioms of agreement: "see eye to eye", "in tune with", "of one mind", "hit it off".

• Opposite idioms: "at loggerheads", "at odds with", "at cross purposes".

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Bite the dust
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To suffer a defeat.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to bite the dust" means to be defeated, to fail, to come to an end, or (in some contexts) to die. (हार जाना / परास्त होना)

◦ Example: Another small shop bit the dust when the mall opened nearby.

◦ Example: The champion finally bit the dust in the semi-final.

• The literal picture is of a fallen warrior lying face down and taking dust into the mouth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "To fall from a height" is only the literal image, not the idiomatic meaning.

• Option 3 "To remain calm" corresponds to idioms like "keep one's cool" or "hold your horses".

• Option 4 "To fall asleep" corresponds to "hit the sack / hit the hay".

NOTE

• Similar idioms of defeat/failure: "go down in flames", "come a cropper", "meet one's Waterloo", "throw in the towel" (to give up).

• Idioms of success (opposite): "come out on top", "carry the day", "with flying colours".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A person who avoids sensory pleasures and physical comforts
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Ascetic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "ascetic" is a person who practises severe self-discipline and abstains from all forms of indulgence, sensory pleasure and physical comfort, usually for religious or spiritual reasons. (तपस्वी / संन्यासी)

◦ Example: The ascetic lived on fruit and water in a mountain cave.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Frugal" is an adjective meaning sparing/economical with money and food (मितव्ययी). It refers to thrift, not to renouncing pleasure on principle.

• Option 2 "Epicurean" is the exact opposite — a person devoted to sensual enjoyment, especially good food and drink (भोगवादी).

• Option 3 "Bohemian" is a person who lives an unconventional, artistic and socially free lifestyle — not one who denies himself comforts.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes frequently asked in SSC exams:

◦ Hermit / Recluse – one who lives alone, away from society

◦ Stoic – one who endures pain or hardship without complaint

◦ Hedonist – one who believes pleasure is the chief good in life

◦ Misanthrope – one who hates mankind

◦ Philanthropist – one who loves and helps mankind

• Word family: ascetic (noun/adjective) – asceticism (noun) – ascetically (adverb).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Conffess.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Conffess" is misspelt — it has a wrongly doubled "f". The correct spelling is "confess", meaning to admit or acknowledge one's fault, crime or secret. (स्वीकार करना / कबूल करना)

◦ Spelling key: CON + FESS (one "f", double "s").

◦ Example: The accused finally confessed to the theft.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "Chivalrous" (Option 1) is correctly spelt — it means courteous, gallant and honourable, especially towards women (शिष्ट / वीर).

• "Expose" (Option 2) is correctly spelt — to uncover, reveal or make something visible (उजागर करना).

• "Convict" (Option 4) is correctly spelt — as a verb, to declare someone guilty; as a noun, a person found guilty of a crime (दोषी ठहराना / अपराधी).

NOTE

• Word family of confess: confess (verb) – confession (noun) – confessor (noun) – confessedly (adverb).

• Watch out for common double-letter traps: necessary (one "c", two "s"), accommodate (two "c", two "m"), occurrence (two "c", two "r"), embarrass (two "r", two "s").

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A person living in solitude like a saint for religious practices.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Hermit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "hermit" is a person who lives alone in solitude, away from society, usually for religious reasons. (संन्यासी / एकांतवासी)

◦ Example: The old hermit had not spoken to anyone for twenty years.

• The definition given — "living in solitude like a saint for religious practices" — is the textbook meaning of a hermit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Cretin" is a very stupid or foolish person (an offensive term) — unrelated to solitude.

• Option 3 "Heir" is a person legally entitled to inherit the property or rank of another (उत्तराधिकारी).

• Option 4 "Heretic" is a person whose belief goes against the accepted doctrine of a religion (विधर्मी) — a hermit follows religion, a heretic opposes its orthodoxy.

NOTE

• Closely related one-word substitutes:

◦ Recluse – a person who lives alone and avoids other people

◦ Ascetic – one who abstains from worldly pleasures for spiritual reasons

◦ Monk / Nun – a member of a religious community

◦ Pilgrim – one who travels to a holy place

◦ Martyr – one who dies for a cause or faith

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Clumsy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Graceful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Clumsy" means awkward in movement or handling things; lacking skill or grace. (भद्दा / अनाड़ी)

• Its antonym is "graceful", meaning moving in a smooth, elegant and attractive way. (सुंदर / लालित्यपूर्ण)

◦ Example: The clumsy waiter dropped the tray, while the graceful dancer glided across the stage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Jealous" means resentful of someone else's success or possessions (ईर्ष्यालु) — unrelated to physical co-ordination.

• Option 2 "Fierce" means violent, aggressive or intense (उग्र) — unrelated.

• Option 4 "Nervous" means anxious or easily agitated (घबराया हुआ). Nervousness may cause clumsiness, but it is not its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of clumsy: awkward, ungainly, gawky, bungling, maladroit, inept, lumbering.

• Antonyms of clumsy: graceful, dexterous, deft, adroit, nimble, agile, skilful.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

No sooner had the sun risen over the horizon when the birds began to chirp and the squirrels started to scamper around the park.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. than the birds began.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "No sooner" is always followed by "than", never by "when" or "then". The fixed pair is "No sooner ... than ...".

• Also, "No sooner" at the beginning of a sentence causes inversion — the auxiliary comes before the subject ("No sooner had the sun risen"), which the sentence has already done correctly.

• Tense sequence: the first clause is in the past perfect ("had risen"), so the clause after "than" must be in the simple past — "began", not "begin".

• The definite article "the" is needed before "birds" because specific birds of that place are meant, matching "the squirrels" later in the sentence.

◦ Correct: No sooner had the sun risen over the horizon than the birds began to chirp and the squirrels started to scamper around the park.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "when the birds begin" keeps the wrong conjunction "when" and also uses the present tense "begin".

• Option 2 "than birds begin" has the right conjunction but a wrong tense ("begin") and drops "the".

• Option 3 "when birds began" keeps the wrong conjunction "when" and drops "the".

NOTE

• Important conjunction pairs for SSC exams:

◦ No sooner ... than – No sooner did he sit down than the phone rang.

◦ Hardly / Scarcely ... when (or before) – Hardly had he sat down when the phone rang.

◦ Barely ... when – Barely had we started when it rained.

◦ Such ... that, So ... that, Rather ... than, Not only ... but also, Lest ... should

• Remember: "No sooner" takes "than", but "Hardly/Scarcely" take "when/before".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

During the meeting, he went on a long and angry _______ about how the project was being mismanaged.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. rant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "rant" is a long, loud, angry speech of complaint or criticism. (लंबा गुस्से भरा भाषण)

• The adjectives "long and angry" and the collocation "went on a ... rant" fix the answer — one "goes on a rant" about something one is furious about.

◦ Correct: During the meeting, he went on a long and angry rant about how the project was being mismanaged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "shout" is a single loud cry, not a long continuous speech; "a long shout" does not collocate with "went on a".

• Option 2 "whisper" is speech in a very soft voice — it contradicts "angry" and "long".

• Option 4 "mutter" is low, indistinct, half-audible speech — again the opposite of a loud outburst.

NOTE

• Collocations: "go on a rant", "rant and rave" (to speak angrily and at length).

• Synonyms of rant: tirade, diatribe, harangue, fulmination, outburst.

• Word family: rant (noun/verb) – ranting (adjective/noun) – ranter (noun).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

I had / a bad habit of / waking up / lately.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. lately.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Lately" means "recently / in the recent past" (हाल ही में) — it is an adverb of time, not of manner.

• The sense required here is "waking up late" (i.e., not early). "Late" itself works both as an adjective and as an adverb of time, so no "-ly" is needed.

◦ Incorrect: I had a bad habit of waking up lately.

◦ Correct: I had a bad habit of waking up late.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "I had" is a correct subject + verb combination in the past tense.

• "a bad habit of" is a correct noun phrase — "habit" is always followed by the preposition "of".

• "waking up" is correct because a preposition ("of") must be followed by a gerund (V-ing).

NOTE

• Adverbs that change meaning when "-ly" is added (a favourite SSC topic):

◦ late (not on time) vs lately (recently)

◦ hard (with effort) vs hardly (almost not)

◦ near (close) vs nearly (almost)

◦ short (abruptly) vs shortly (soon)

◦ high (at a great height) vs highly (very much)

◦ most (superlative) vs mostly (mainly)

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Chaitnya was __________ from the school due to his misappropriate behaviour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. expelled.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Expelled" means officially forced to leave a school, organisation or country as a punishment. (निष्कासित करना / निकाल देना)

• It is the only correctly spelt option: EX + PEL + LED — the final "l" of "expel" is doubled before "-ed" because the verb ends in a single consonant preceded by a stressed vowel.

◦ Correct: Chaitnya was expelled from the school due to his misappropriate behaviour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Options 2 "xpelled" and 4 "xpeled" wrongly drop the initial "e".

• Option 3 "expeled" wrongly uses a single "l" before "-ed".

NOTE

• Doubling rule: for verbs ending in a single vowel + single consonant with the stress on the last syllable, double the final consonant before "-ed/-ing" — expel → expelled/expelling, compel → compelled, refer → referred, prefer → preferred, begin → beginning, permit → permitted.

• Word family: expel (verb) – expulsion (noun) – expelled (past/participle). Related words: rusticate (to suspend a student temporarily), suspend, debar, oust, banish.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once there was a king named Midas who was granted a (1)________ by Dionysus, the god of wine. For his wish, Midas asked that whatever he (2)________ would turn to gold. Despite Dionysus’ efforts to prevent it, Midas pleaded that this was a fantastic wish, and so, it was bestowed. Excited about his newly-earned (3)________, Midas started touching all kinds of things, turning each item into pure gold. But soon, Midas became (4)________. As he picked up a piece of food, he found he couldn’t eat it. It had turned to gold in his hand. Hungry, Midas groaned, “I’ll starve! Perhaps this was not such an excellent wish after all!” Seeing his dismay, Midas’ (5)________ daughter threw her arms around him to comfort him, and she, too, turned to gold. “The golden touch is no blessing,” Midas cried.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. wish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is what Dionysus granted to King Midas. The very next sentence begins, "For his wish, Midas asked that whatever he touched would turn to gold." That reference back ("his wish") makes "wish" the only possible filler.

◦ Correct: Once there was a king named Midas who was granted a wish by Dionysus, the god of wine.

• The collocation "granted a wish" is a fixed expression in folk tales and mythology.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "slavery" (the state of being owned by another) is negative and completely out of context for a divine boon.

• Options 3 "employment" and 4 "job" refer to paid work; a god does not grant a king a "job", and neither word is echoed anywhere in the passage.

NOTE

• Contextual clue technique: in cloze passages, look for the word or idea repeated immediately after the blank. Here "For his wish" is a direct give-away.

• Collocations with "grant": grant a wish, grant permission, grant a request, grant a loan, take something for granted.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Once there was a king named Midas who was granted a (1)________ by Dionysus, the god of wine. For his wish, Midas asked that whatever he (2)________ would turn to gold. Despite Dionysus’ efforts to prevent it, Midas pleaded that this was a fantastic wish, and so, it was bestowed. Excited about his newly-earned (3)________, Midas started touching all kinds of things, turning each item into pure gold. But soon, Midas became (4)________. As he picked up a piece of food, he found he couldn’t eat it. It had turned to gold in his hand. Hungry, Midas groaned, “I’ll starve! Perhaps this was not such an excellent wish after all!” Seeing his dismay, Midas’ (5)________ daughter threw her arms around him to comfort him, and she, too, turned to gold. “The golden touch is no blessing,” Midas cried.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. touched.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The whole legend is about the "golden touch" of King Midas — whatever he touched turned to gold. The passage itself confirms this twice: "Midas started touching all kinds of things, turning each item into pure gold" and the closing line, "The golden touch is no blessing."

◦ Correct: For his wish, Midas asked that whatever he touched would turn to gold.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "next felt" is grammatically clumsy and makes no sense in the clause "whatever he next felt would turn to gold".

• Option 3 "kept" (retained) and Option 4 "left" (abandoned/departed from) contradict the later sentences, where the gold appears the moment he picks an object up, not when he keeps or leaves it.

NOTE

• General knowledge link: the expression "the Midas touch" is used today for a person who succeeds at, and profits from, everything he undertakes.

• Tense clue: the reporting structure "asked that whatever he ______ would turn" requires a simple past verb, which "touched", "kept" and "left" all satisfy — so the decision must be made on meaning, and only "touched" matches the story.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. powers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Midas has just been given a supernatural ability — the ability to turn objects into gold by touch. Such an ability is called a "power". "Excited about his newly-earned powers", he begins testing it on everything.

◦ Correct: Excited about his newly-earned powers, Midas started touching all kinds of things, turning each item into pure gold.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "legacies" means things handed down from an ancestor or predecessor; Midas's gift came from a god as a boon, and it is described as "newly-earned", not inherited.

• Option 3 "awards" are prizes given for achievement or merit — Midas won no contest.

• Option 4 "visuals" means images or pictures — meaningless here.

NOTE

• Collocations with "power": supernatural powers, magical powers, the power to do something, come to power, in power, power of attorney.

• Note the adjective "newly-earned" — the hyphenated compound modifies the noun that follows, so a noun is required in the blank; all four options are nouns, so the choice depends on meaning.

• Both "Hungry" and "I'll starve" are direct textual clues, so "hungry" is the word that fits blank 4.

◦ Correct: But soon, Midas became hungry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Options 1 "mad" and 4 "angry" describe rage; the passage shows dismay and helplessness, and the food-and-starvation detail points specifically to hunger.

• Option 3 "tired" (needing rest) is not supported anywhere in the passage.

NOTE

• Cloze strategy: read one or two sentences beyond the blank. Here the word "Hungry" is literally repeated later, confirming the answer.

• Vocabulary: starve = to suffer or die from lack of food (भूखा मरना); famished / ravenous = extremely hungry; satiated = fully satisfied with food.

Despite Dionysus’ efforts to prevent it, Midas pleaded that this was a fantastic wish, and so, it was bestowed. Excited about his newly-earned (3)________, Midas started touching all kinds of things, turning each item into pure gold. But soon, Midas became (4)________. As he picked up a piece of food, he found he couldn’t eat it. It had turned to gold in his hand. Hungry, Midas groaned, “I’ll starve! Perhaps this was not such an excellent wish after all!” Seeing his dismay, Midas’ (5)________ daughter threw her arms around him to comfort him, and she, too, turned to gold. “The golden touch is no blessing,” Midas cried.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. beloved.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The daughter "threw her arms around him to comfort him" when she saw her father's dismay. Such affection shows that she was dearly loved, so the adjective needed is "beloved" — much loved, dear to the heart. (प्रियतम / अत्यंत प्रिय)

◦ Correct: Seeing his dismay, Midas' beloved daughter threw her arms around him to comfort him ...

• The word also heightens the tragedy of the story: the thing he loved most is destroyed by his own greed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "estranged" means no longer close or affectionate, alienated — it contradicts the loving embrace.

• Option 2 "guarded" means cautious/protected; it does not describe a relationship of love.

• Option 4 "hated" is the direct opposite of the emotion shown in the sentence.

NOTE

• Synonyms of beloved: dear, cherished, adored, treasured, darling, precious.

• Antonyms: hated, detested, loathed, despised, estranged.

• Moral of the story: greed brings ruin; hence the closing line, "The golden touch is no blessing."
